document.title: IAC Intelligence Assessment IA 7/96 - Afghanistan: Taliban's Challenges, Regional Concerns
document.authors: Privy Council Office (Ottawa, Canada), released by U.S. National Security Agency
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
document.note: [Top Secret - SI, Umbra] Canadian assessment a month after the Taliban takeover of Kabul. It sees a country divided between Pakistan-supported Pushtun/Taliban forces and the Tajik/Uzbek/Shia forces of Dostam, Masood and Khalili. Regional neighbors fear the Taliban, and even Pakistan must harbour concern about Taliban links to its own Pashtuns. Kashmiri militants will likely be encouraged.

persons.role: Former defence minister; Tajik commander controlling the Panjshir Valley; anti-Taliban alliance partner

mentions.quote: FORMER DEFENCE MINISTER AHMED SHAH MASOOD AND HIS TAJIK FORCES STILL CONTROL THE DIFFICULT TERRAIN OF THE PANJSHIR VALLEY.
THIS ALLIANCE PROVIDED ENCOURAGEMENT TO MASOOD'S FORCES, WHO HAVE CARRIED THE BRUNT OF THE MOST RECENT FIGHTING NORTH OF KABUL.
TALIBAN LEADERS HAVE SAID THEY WILL NOT NEGOTIATE WITH MASOOD BUT ARE PREPARED TO TALK WITH DOSTAM

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Extreme fundamentalist Sunni, mainly Pushtun movement; captured Kabul and set up a six-man interim shura; described as Pakistan-supported.

organizations.name: National Islamic Movement
organizations.notes: Mainly Uzbek force of General Dostam controlling the northern provinces; supported by Uzbekistan and, in the past, limited support from Turkmenistan.

organizations.name: Hezb-i-Wahdat
organizations.notes: Shia Hazara party of Karim Khalili based in Bamyan; joined the 9 Oct 1996 alliance.

organizations.name: Rabbani government
organizations.notes: Ousted from Kabul; its officials still represent Afghanistan at the UN; Dostam recognised its legitimacy.

organizations.name: United Nations
organizations.notes: Tried to broker rapprochement since March 1994; UN compound sheltered Najibullah.

organizations.name: UN Security Council
organizations.notes: Debate of 16 Oct 1996 adjourned without a date for resumption.

organizations.name: UN Credentials Committee
organizations.notes: Decides Afghan representation at the UN; Russia has a vote and it is unlikely to consider a Taliban application.

organizations.name: Commonwealth of Independent States
organizations.notes: Russia regards the Afghan strife as a direct threat; the 1992 CIS Collective Security Treaty; Turkmenistan is not a party.

organizations.name: Russian government
organizations.notes: Convened the 4 Oct 1996 meeting of Central Asian leaders; called for resistance by Masood and Dostam.

organizations.name: Government of Pakistan
organizations.notes: Seen as supporter of the Pushtun/Taliban forces; wants a friendly Kabul government to open trade routes to Central Asia.

organizations.name: Government of Iran
organizations.notes: Seen as a potential supporter of anti-Taliban elements; supports the anti-Taliban bloc.

organizations.name: Government of India
organizations.notes: Supports the anti-Taliban bloc; worried about Kashmir militants being encouraged by Taliban successes.

organizations.name: Government of Uzbekistan
organizations.notes: Supports Dostam as an ethnic Uzbek; fears spillover of fundamentalism.

organizations.name: Government of Turkmenistan
organizations.notes: Provided limited past support to Dostam; most openly advocates a negotiated settlement; interested in a gas pipeline via Afghanistan to Pakistan.

organizations.name: Government of Tajikistan
organizations.notes: Its president pressed for formal CIS support of the anti-Taliban forces of Dostam and Masood.

organizations.name: Kashmiri militants
aliases: Militants resisting Indian control of Kashmir
organizations.notes: Unnamed groups assessed as encouraged by Taliban successes.

events.description: UN begins unsuccessful efforts to facilitate rapprochement among warring Afghan factions.
Early 1995: signs that Afghan leaders might accept the UN plan for an interim authority; plan ultimately failed over Taliban and Rabbani demands.
Taliban capture Kabul, ousting the Rabbani government, and set up a six-man interim shura with a separate commission to govern the capital.
Taliban kill former president Najibullah, who had sanctuary in the UN compound.
Russia convenes a meeting of leaders from four Central Asian countries; promises only an 'appropriate response' to threats to the CIS border and calls for a ceasefire under UN auspices.
Defensive military alliance formed by Dostam, Masood and Karim Khalili against the Taliban.
UN Security Council debate on Afghanistan adjourned without a date for resumption.
IAC Intelligence Assessment IA 7/96 approved.

Russia convened a meeting of leaders from four Central Asian countries on Afghanistan; promised only an 'appropriate response' to threats to the CIS border and called for ceasefire and UN-auspices settlement.
Turkmenistan's president did not attend the Oct 4 meeting.
Taliban capture of Kabul, referenced as background.
Alliance formed between Dostam, Masood and Khalili (Hezb-i-Wahdat) against the Taliban.
UN begins unsuccessful efforts to facilitate rapprochement among Afghan factions.
Early 1995: signs that Afghan leaders were prepared to accept the UN plan for an interim authority; the plan ultimately failed.
Taliban killed former president Najibullah after capturing Kabul.
Russia-arranged meeting of leaders of four Central Asian countries; promised 'appropriate response' to threats to the CIS border and called for ceasefire under UN auspices.
Taliban captured Kabul, ousting the Rabbani government.
Dostam, Masood and Khalili formed a defensive military alliance against the Taliban.
Alliance counter-attacks on Taliban forces north of Kabul, initially successful, followed by Taliban reversals.
Taliban established a six-man interim shura in Kabul with a separate commission to govern the capital.

sources_cited: IAC Intelligence Assessment IA 7/96 (Canadian Privy Council Office), approved 17 Oct 1996, released by NSA under FOIA Case 41856
key_claims: Taliban capture of Kabul does not presage peace; the Taliban will find it difficult to extend control militarily to the north.
Afghanistan could divide into Pakistan-supported Pushtun/Taliban forces and Tajik/Uzbek/Shia forces of Dostam, Masood and Hezb-i-Wahdat backed by Iran, Russia, India and Central Asian states.
Dostam, Masood and Karim Khalili formed a defensive alliance on 9 October 1996 that produced initial counter-attacks north of Kabul.
Taliban is unlikely to moderate its strict Islamic policies and is unlikely to accept a further UN brokering role; the killing of Najibullah showed scant respect for the UN.
Taliban is unlikely to systematically export fundamentalism, but encouragement of Islamic insurgents in Central Asia will irritate neighbours.
Pakistan seeks a friendly Kabul government to open trade routes to Central Asia but may worry about a Pushtun government calling for 'Greater Pushtunistan' and about a prolonged stalemate.
Russia and Uzbekistan fear Taliban-inspired fundamentalism; Russia urged resistance by Masood and Dostam, while Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan favour negotiated settlement.
